clue.text: Fish and chops left in slices

indicators.note: the word in tells us the letter for left goes inside the fish-and-chops pair

parts.note: the cod is a common food fish
chops as a verb means cuts

explanation.surface: A fishmonger's order: fish, and some chops, sliced and left in the window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish and chops' sounds like a takeaway order, but the two words are separate pieces, and 'in' slips the left letter between the fish's second and third letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold cuts are thin slices of cooked meat served chilled, so the plural phrase means sliced cooked meats.

clue.text: Shared riches with Doris for 24 hours in march

parts.note: something shared by all is held in common
riches means wealth
Doris Day was the American singer and film actress

explanation.surface: Someone shares their fortune with a woman called Doris for a day during a protest march.
explanation.walkthrough: 'march' looks like a protest walk, but the lower-case word is the month of March: Commonwealth Day falls on the second Monday of March.
explanation.definitionFit: Commonwealth Day is the annual observance of the British Commonwealth, held on a single day in the month of March.

clue.text: Gross periodical finally has Mrs Simpson topless

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word periodical
topless means the word loses its top, i.e. its opening letter, in a down clue

parts.note: Marge Simpson is the wife of Homer in the cartoon The Simpsons

explanation.surface: A gross magazine finally runs a topless picture of a cartoon housewife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mrs Simpson' suggests Wallis Simpson, but it is Marge from The Simpsons; 'topless' strips her M, leaving ARGE after the L from 'periodical'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gross in the sense of big or bulky is a synonym of large, as in a gross figure.

clue.text: Cards he shuffled wanting a game

indicators.note: cards are shuffled to mix them, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A card player shuffles the pack but would rather play something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting a' reads as lacking an A, but here it means wanting to have one: the letters of CARDS HE plus A are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Charades is a parlour game in which players mime words for others to guess.

clue.text: Attempted to be heard in court

explanation.surface: Someone tried to get their case heard before a judge.
explanation.definitionFit: Attempted means had a go at something; a case heard in court has been judged by a judge or jury.

clue.text: Canadian city? We hear pilots queue for it

definitions.text: We hear pilots queue for it

explanation.surface: A question about a Canadian city, then a remark about pilots lining up to fly there.
explanation.walkthrough: In the NATO phonetic alphabet pilots say this city's name for the letter Q, which is said like 'queue'; 'We hear' tells you the queue is the letter's sound, not a line of people.
explanation.definitionFit: The city is the capital of a Canadian province, and its name is the radio code word for the seventeenth letter.

clue.text: Open a tent, perhaps

parts.note: tent is also a dark red Spanish wine, so opening a tent means pulling the stopper from a wine bottle

explanation.surface: Unzipping a tent on a camping trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Tent here is not canvas but a sweet red Spanish wine, once used as communion wine; to open a bottle of it you remove the stopper.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull the stopper out of a wine bottle is to open it, and tent is one such wine.

clue.text: Prohibit aetist with partially digested food and a fish

parts.note: to bar something is to prohibit it
a misprint of artist; RA, Royal Academician, stands for an artist
cud is the half-digested food a cow brings back up to chew again

explanation.surface: An artist is banned for eating half-chewed food and a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aetist' is a typing slip for 'artist' in the clue as held; the artist is RA, a member of the Royal Academy.
explanation.definitionFit: The barracuda is a long predatory sea fish with sharp teeth.

clue.text: Before start of dusk tribe capture noisy bats in fantastic place

indicators.note: Before says the tribe-and-captives group comes ahead of the next letter
the tribe captures, i.e. holds inside it, the noisy bats

parts.note: a clan is a tribe or family group
noisy means loud
bats is slang for mad, as is cuckoo

indicators.note: start of picks the opening letter of the word dusk

explanation.surface: At nightfall a tribe catches screeching bats in a fairy-tale land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bats' looks like the flying animals; it is the adjective meaning crazy. 'Before' puts the tribe, holding the noisy pair, ahead of the dusk letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase, from Aristophanes' play The Birds, names an imaginary ideal realm of fanciful, unrealistic dreams.

clue.text: End up round a toppled pine tree

indicators.note: round says the first part goes around the rest
in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal

indicators.note: toppled means knocked over, so the word is turned backwards

parts.note: to pine for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: Someone finishes beside a pine tree that has fallen over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pine' looks like the tree but is the verb to yearn. 'up' turns the end word to MIA and 'toppled' turns the pine word to GNOL; 'round' wraps the first round A plus the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The magnolia is a flowering tree or shrub with large showy blooms.

clue.text: One leaving tia Maria with German runs off for another drink

indicators.note: off means the letters go awry and are rearranged
One leaving means the letter for one departs from the liqueur's name

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: At the bar, someone abandons a coffee liqueur and a German friend to go for a different cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: Tia Maria is a coffee liqueur. Remove one I to leave TAMARIA, add G and R, and 'off' rearranges the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A margarita is a cocktail of tequila, lime and orange liqueur, so it is a mixed alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Load vehicle with board game

parts.note: a car is a motor vehicle
go is the ancient Asian board game played with black and white stones

explanation.surface: A car is loaded up with a board game for a family trip.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo is the freight carried by a ship or plane, so it means a load of goods.

clue.text: Game played at front of oval is last of series

indicators.note: front of picks the opening letter of the word oval
played means the letters of game are put into play and rearranged

explanation.surface: A cricket match at the Oval decides the final fixture of a series.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a London cricket ground, so the surface paints a Test series finale; 'played' rearranges the game letters and the oval's first letter goes at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the final letter of the Greek alphabet, so it stands for the end of any sequence.

clue.text: Authority to leave if late?

parts.note: late here means dead, and leave means bequeath body organs; the document gives permission for that

explanation.surface: A note that lets an employee go home if they are running behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' reads as behind schedule but means deceased, and 'leave' means hand on organs after death, not go away.
explanation.definitionFit: A small card carried to show consent that one's organs may be used for transplant after death.

clue.text: With training we backed healthy swimmer

indicators.note: training puts the letters of with through a drill that reshapes them
backed means the word we is read in reverse

parts.note: hale means healthy, as in hale and hearty

explanation.surface: A swimmer trained hard and we supported a fit athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'training' rearranges the With letters into WHIT and 'backed' turns we into EW. The swimmer is Moby-Dick from Melville's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Moby-Dick is the albino sperm whale of Melville's novel, and a whale is a creature that swims.

clue.text: One can't go out at nights

definitions.text: One can't go out at nights

parts.words: One can't go out at nights
parts.note: go out here means drop off to sleep, as a light goes out, not leave the house

explanation.surface: Someone housebound who cannot leave home after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go out' suggests a night on the town; it means fall unconscious in sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A sufferer from chronic sleeplessness lies awake through the night unable to drop off.

clue.text: Indian chief we hear is more senior — what a change!

indicators.note: we hear tells us a word is given for how it is said rather than spelt

parts.note: someone more senior ranks higher

indicators.note: change means the letters of what a are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at how much a superior has changed.
explanation.walkthrough: HIGHER said in a non-rhotic British accent sounds like HIA; WATHA is the anagram of WHAT A. The chief is the Native American leader of Longfellow's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The Onondaga leader celebrated in Longfellow's epic poem was a Native American, called Indian in older usage.

clue.text: Wise leader returned carpet to university

indicators.note: returned means the word for carpet comes back in reverse

parts.note: a rug is a small carpet

explanation.surface: A sage brings a borrowed carpet back to college.
explanation.definitionFit: A guru is a spiritual teacher or mentor whose wisdom followers seek.

clue.text: Phone doctor up about primarily organising a bypass

parts.note: to ring someone is to phone them

indicators.note: about says the doctor goes around the next letters
in a down clue, up means the word is read bottom to top
primarily picks the opening letter of the word organising

explanation.surface: Phoning a doctor to get them organised about a heart bypass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bypass' looks surgical, beside a doctor; it is a road round a town. DR turned up gives RD, which goes round O and A.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring road circles a town so traffic can avoid the centre, which is what a bypass does.

clue.text: Some despair about part of church

indicators.note: about means the run of letters is turned round
Some means only a portion of the word despair is used

explanation.surface: A churchgoer feels a degree of despair.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the semicircular recess at the east end of a church, usually behind the altar.

clue.text: Zebra crossing here in Longleat?

parts.note: a zebra crossing is a British striped pedestrian crossing, but here it means a real striped animal walking across a wildlife park

explanation.surface: Asking whether a pedestrian crossing exists at a stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: A zebra crossing is a British black-and-white striped road crossing; Longleat is a Wiltshire stately home famous for its drive-through animal park.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclosure where wild animals roam freely and visitors drive through to see them, as at Longleat.

clue.text: Leave claim to reward

explanation.surface: Someone abandons their claim to a prize.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave or abandon a post is to run away from it; one's just deserts are what one merits, a claim to recompense.

clue.text: Mild ruler losing gold in the gallery

indicators.note: in says the trimmed ruler is placed inside the gallery's name

parts.note: the Tate is the famous London art gallery

indicators.note: losing means the ruler's word gives up the letters for gold

parts.note: an emperor is a ruler
OR is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A gentle monarch loses his gold in an art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' leaves EMPER once the gold is taken from the ruler, and 'in' puts that inside the gallery, London's Tate.
explanation.definitionFit: A temperate climate is mild, without extremes of heat or cold.

clue.text: Part of fire dropping hot dirt

indicators.note: dropping means the letter for hot is let fall from the word

parts.note: the hearth is the floor of a fireplace, part of where a fire burns
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A fire dies down and its embers fall as soot.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth means soil or ground, which is loose dirt.

clue.text: Send back approval about, say, a lizard

indicators.note: Send back means the whole string of letters is reversed

parts.note: OK signals approval
C, for circa, means about
EG, for example, means say

explanation.surface: Someone returns a request for approval, citing a lizard as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: OK, C and EG are reversed together.
explanation.definitionFit: The gecko is a small nocturnal lizard of warm regions with sticky toe pads.

clue.text: Endlessly boast about brilliant city

indicators.note: about says the trimmed boast goes around the next letters
Endlessly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: to crow is to boast
A1 means first-rate, brilliant, written here as A and I

explanation.surface: Someone keeps boasting about a dazzling city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' leaves CRO; brilliant is A1, first-class, written with the letter I standing for the figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Cairo is the capital of Egypt, a city on the Nile.

clue.text: Urge to take a long golf shot

explanation.surface: A golfer feels the urge to hit a long one.
explanation.definitionFit: Drive as a noun is an urge or impulse; as a golf verb it means strike the ball from the tee.

clue.text: Old chairman sacked? Blow me!

indicators.note: sacked means the chairman is thrown out, scattering the letters

explanation.surface: Astonishment at the news that a long-serving company boss has been fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow me!' looks like an exclamation of surprise; read literally it is an instrument asking to be blown.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouth organ is a wind instrument played by blowing, so the exclamation invites you to play one.

clue.text: Guy returned installing central heating in boats

indicators.note: installing means the heating is put inside the reversed word
returned means the word is read backwards

parts.note: a guy is a rope or stay used to steady a mast or tent

explanation.surface: A man comes home to fit central heating in his boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' reads as a man; it is a guy rope, a stay, which 'returned' turns into YATS before 'installing' adds the heating abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Yachts are sailing or motor vessels used for racing or cruising.

clue.text: Has doled out a big amount

indicators.note: out means the letters are dealt out and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone has handed out a large sum.
explanation.definitionFit: Shedload is British slang for a large quantity, a great deal.
